candidato.titulo: Targeted radioactive therapy may help delay spread of recurrent prostate cancer
candidato.resumo: Adding the targeted radioactive drug 177Lu-PNT2002 to stereotactic body radiation therapy, or SBRT, may help keep recurrent prostate cancer under control longer than SBRT alone, according to new research led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

texto_fonte:
Targeted radioactive therapy may help delay spread of recurrent prostate cancer
Adding the targeted radioactive drug 177Lu-PNT2002 to stereotactic body radiation therapy, or SBRT, may help keep recurrent prostate cancer under control longer than SBRT alone, according to new research led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.
The team found patients who received the combination were less likely to develop widespread disease or hormone-resistant cancer, suggesting the treatment may offer benefits beyond delaying the initial return of the disease.
The findings, published in the journal European Urology, come from an updated analysis of the phase 2 LUNAR trial, which followed men for nearly three years after their prostate cancer had returned and was detected in a limited number of sites.
"Our earlier findings showed that adding 177Lu-PNT2002 could significantly delay progression and the need for hormone therapy," said Dr. Amar Kishan, executive vice chair of radiation oncology at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and first author of the study.
"But with longer follow-up, we're seeing signs that the benefit may extend beyond simply delaying recurrence, including a potential reduction in the risk of widespread disease and cancer that no longer responds to hormone therapy. These findings suggest we may be able to treat cancer cells that are present elsewhere in the body but are too small to detect, while giving patients more time before they need hormone therapy."
Targeting cancer too small to detect
For some men with prostate cancer, the disease returns after initial treatment and can be detected in only a few locations. Doctors can use SBRT to target and destroy those visible tumors. But cancer cells may also be present elsewhere in the body at levels too small to be detected even by highly sensitive PSMA PET scans.
Because 177Lu-PNT2002 travels through the bloodstream and targets PSMA, a protein found on most prostate cancer cells, the treatment may be able to reach some of this otherwise undetectable disease.
The approach could be particularly important for patients who want to delay hormone therapy. Although hormone therapy can control recurrent prostate cancer, long-term treatment can cause side effects and affect quality of life.
Testing the combination in recurrent disease
The LUNAR trial included 92 men with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, meaning their cancer had returned and spread to one to five sites that could be identified on PSMA PET/CT and treated with SBRT.
The patients were randomly assigned to receive either SBRT alone or two cycles of 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The cycles of radioactive treatment were given about eight weeks apart, with SBRT administered after the second cycle.
The researchers followed the patients for a median of 31.9 months. They evaluated progression-free survival, as well as several additional measures of how the cancer progressed, including whether patients developed more widespread disease, castration-resistant prostate cancer or progression on conventional imaging.
Lower progression risk with longer follow-up
The longer follow-up continued to show a benefit from adding 177Lu-PNT2002 to SBRT. The risk of progression or needing additional hormone therapy was 62% lower in the combination group than in the SBRT-alone group.
At 24 months, 33% of patients who received 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT had no detectable disease, compared with 12% of those who received SBRT alone.
The researchers also found fewer patients in the combination group developed widespread disease. Three patients receiving 177Lu-PNT2002 and SBRT developed more than five new cancer sites, compared with nine patients who received SBRT alone.
Similarly, one patient in the combination group developed castration-resistant prostate cancer, compared with seven patients in the SBRT-alone group. Because these were exploratory analyses with relatively few events, the findings will need to be confirmed in larger studies.
The combination also showed a trend toward longer control of disease on conventional imaging, which is used to detect larger or more established tumors.
In the earlier analysis of the trial, patients who received 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT went a median of 17.6 months without progression or the need for additional hormone therapy, compared with 7.4 months for those who received SBRT alone.
The researchers observed no new safety signals with longer follow-up, and serious treatment-related side effects remained uncommon.
Earlier treatment warrants further study
For patients whose prostate cancer has returned in only a few places, the goal of treatment is often to control the visible tumors while delaying the need for hormone therapy and preventing the cancer from spreading more widely.
The findings suggest that combining a treatment that targets visible tumors with a radioactive drug that travels throughout the body may offer a way to address both visible and microscopic disease.
"This is an important step toward understanding whether we can use these treatments earlier, when the amount of cancer in the body is still relatively small," Kishan said.
The researchers say the findings support further study of PSMA-targeted radioligand therapy earlier in the course of prostate cancer, before patients develop more advanced or treatment-resistant disease.
Publication details
Amar U. Kishan et al., 177Lu-Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Prior to Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy in Oligorecurrent Prostate Cancer: Secondary and Exploratory End Point Results from the Randomized Phase 2 LUNAR Trial, European Urology (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.eururo.2026.09.005
Journal information: European Urology

candidato.titulo: How cells make their command center accessible
candidato.resumo: The cells of higher organisms such as mammals, flies and fungi enclose their genetic material in a nucleus. A nuclear envelope, consisting of two stacked membranes, protects it. For the cell to survive, the nucleus must constantly exchange molecules with the rest of the cell. This exchange relies on channels called nuclear pores, which act as selective gates that transport proteins or messenger RNA in or out.

texto_fonte:
How cells make their command center accessible
The cells of higher organisms such as mammals, flies and fungi enclose their genetic material in a nucleus. A nuclear envelope, consisting of two stacked membranes, protects it. For the cell to survive, the nucleus must constantly exchange molecules with the rest of the cell. This exchange relies on channels called nuclear pores, which act as selective gates that transport proteins or messenger RNA in or out.
Before this pore complex can be assembled, the cell must first punch an opening through both membranes and then seamlessly seal the edges. How cells accomplish this was a long-standing puzzle.
Now, research teams at the Institute of Biochemistry, led by ETH professors Ulrike Kutay, Karsten Weis and Madhav Jagannathan, together with colleagues from the University of Fribourg and other partners, have solved the puzzle.
Their findings not only answer a fundamental question in cell biology but also offer an explanation and a potential therapeutic approach for a hereditary form of dystonia, a rare but severe movement disorder. The corresponding studies have been published in the journal Molecular Cell.
A surprising fusion mechanism
The researchers have shown for the first time that two tools are required for the envelope's two membranes to fuse perfectly: the enzyme Torsin-1A and a complex of several CLCC1 units (in humans) or their fungal counterparts, Brl1 and Brr6. Until now, it was known that a defect in Torsin-1A halts nuclear pore assembly—with fatal consequences for the cell.
The researchers show how this cooperation works: Torsin-1A binds to CLCC1 and helps several of these building blocks join together. Torsin-1A then accompanies the CLCC1 complex to the site of pore assembly to enable membrane fusion.
The exact mechanism of the fusion also caught the research teams by surprise. Using computer simulations, they hypothesized that CLCC1 proteins (or their relatives Brl1 and Brr6 in fungi) forge a temporary channel inside the nuclear envelope. This allows fat molecules (lipids) to flow across the bilayers, rendering the local membrane unstable and forcing the fusion of the two nuclear membranes.
"We had not expected such a mechanism," explains the first author of one of the studies, Daria Maslennikova, who completed her doctorate in Kutay's group.
New hope for primary dystonia
These findings shed new light on primary dystonia (DYT1 dystonia), a rare, currently incurable neurological movement disorder. Worldwide, about six in 100,000 people are affected. The disease usually begins in childhood and presents with painful muscle spasms and abnormal postures. To date, the symptoms have been alleviated only through physical therapy or botulinum toxin injections.
In humans with primary dystonia, a mutation in the Torsin1A gene prevents the Torsin1A molecule from functioning correctly, leaving the CLCC1 complex with insufficient support.
Using fruit fly (Drosophila) experiments, the researchers showed that artificially increasing CLCC1 levels can correct defects that occur, for example, during germline cell development.
Why an alteration in the Torsin-1A gene causes symptoms in only about a third of mutation carriers is still unclear, but the researchers speculate that person-specific differences in CLCC1 protein levels may contribute.
A therapeutic approach on the horizon
"This finding helps us envision a possible therapy," explains ETH professor Kutay. One potential treatment strategy could be to boost CLCC1 production or prevent the protein from breaking down. This approach has already shown success in human cell cultures and in fruit flies. Whether these findings can be successfully translated to humans must first be evaluated in further clinical studies and drug screens.
The scientific breakthrough resulted from close collaboration among research groups at ETH Zurich, the University of Fribourg, the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) and RWTH Aachen University. The fact that fundamental cellular discoveries can lead to new therapies highlights the enduring value of basic research.
In the future, the teams plan to investigate additional relatives of the enzyme Torsin1A. Human cells also contain other torsins whose precise functions remain unknown. Kutay, Weis, Jagannathan and their colleagues, working in collaboration with plant scientists, aim to determine whether similar molecules and mechanisms also operate in plants.
Publication details
Daria Maslennikova et al., The dystonia-associated Torsin1A sustains CLCC1 function in membrane fusion of the nuclear envelope for NPC biogenesis, Molecular Cell (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.molcel.2026.07.016
Jonas S. Fischer et al., A conserved mechanism of membrane fusion in nuclear pore complex assembly, Molecular Cell (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.molcel.2026.06.023

candidato.titulo: Q&A: Mars Perseverance Rover Distance Record
candidato.resumo: On October 11 , the Perseverance rover completed a drive that brought its total distance traveled on Mars to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers). This is a new record for Mars rovers, enabled in large part by Perseverance’s ability to drive with much more autonomy than its predecessors. Over the last five years, Perseverance’s autonomy software has been steadily upgraded, and to learn more about how the record was broken and what the future holds for the rover, we spoke with Mark Maimone , the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who designed and developed the self-driving software for Mars rovers Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance. Before we talk about Perseverance, let’s pour one out for the previous record holder Opportunity , which landed on Mars in January of 2004 for a 3-month mission and ended its epic journey 15 years later in February of 2019. This NASA video compresses Opportunity’s entire mission into four minutes, and gives a poignant sense of the incredible distance that this little rover traveled over its 15 year life on Mars, doing science as it went: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory/YouTube Opportunity drove 4

texto_fonte:
On October 11, the Perseverance rover completed a drive that brought its total distance traveled on Mars to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers). This is a new record for Mars rovers, enabled in large part by Perseverance’s ability to drive with much more autonomy than its predecessors. Over the last five years, Perseverance’s autonomy software has been steadily upgraded, and to learn more about how the record was broken and what the future holds for the rover, we spoke with Mark Maimone, the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who designed and developed the self-driving software for Mars rovers Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance.
Before we talk about Perseverance, let’s pour one out for the previous record holder Opportunity, which landed on Mars in January of 2004 for a 3-month mission and ended its epic journey 15 years later in February of 2019. This NASA video compresses Opportunity’s entire mission into four minutes, and gives a poignant sense of the incredible distance that this little rover traveled over its 15 year life on Mars, doing science as it went:
Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers until a planetary-scale dust storm stopped it in its tracks, appropriately enough, in Perseverance Valley.
On Feb. 18, 2021, Perseverance joined NASA’s Curiosity rover on the red planet, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter tucked under its belly. Curiosity and Perseverance both ditched Opportunity’s solar panels for a radioisotope thermoelectric generator. Curiosity has been active on Mars since 2012.
Despite Curiosity’s nearly 10 year head start, Perseverance is the rover to first break Opportunity’s record. There are several reasons for Perseverance overtaking Opportunity—ruggedized wheels for one—but the biggest contributor is that Perseverance was built for autonomy.
To understand how JPL taught a Mars rover to drive itself from 225 million kilometers away without crashing, IEEE Spectrum spoke with Mark Maimone, the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
Let’s talk about rover autonomy on Mars. Even before Perseverance, rovers were driving themselves, right?
Mark Maimone: Yes! Sojourner [in 1997] had an early kind of autonomous behavior—for sensing, it used four laser stripes projected onto the surface, which it used to measure the height of 20 points in the terrain in front of it. It could steer around big obstacles, or even thread the needle between two things. It was a real autonomy system, which is very impressive considering its CPU was less than one megahertz.
With Spirit and Opportunity, I developed the autonomy for those rovers. Every time they drove, they would use 256 x 256 pixel stereo pairs to map the geometry of the terrain and find a safe route forward. Spirit actually ended up driving itself 23% of the time, which I was frankly shocked by, since it drove much more slowly in that mode. But using autonomy helped Spirit travel 50% faster than it otherwise could have. Opportunity and Curiosity both only used autonomous driving about 5% of the time. Perseverance is the first Mars rover that drives itself 90% of the time, with its enhanced autonomy system that includes a second processor with an FPGA to do speed up extra image processing operations.
What was it like to let Perseverance drive itself for the first time?
Maimone: Perseverance is the culmination of decades of work on Mars rover autonomy, so seeing Perseverance use its AutoNav system to drive itself basically at full speed, up to 120 meters an hour, was incredible.
These two images taken by Perseverance’s hazard avoidance and navigation cameras show (on left) the very first AutoNav drive on Mars where the rover autonomously stopped before running into a rock pile, and (on right) the second AutoNav drive where the rover successfully steered around a rock.JPL-Caltech/NASA
Where are the humans in this process?
Maimone: The plan of where to go is specified by the science team, and then on the engineering side, the strategic route planning team develops a path to get us to that goal by guessing, based on lower-resolution maps from orbit, what the terrain is going to look like for the rover. Each day a tactical operations team combines the strategic overall route with that day’s science goals to pick the actual route the rover will follow.
We want humans to keep doing long-range planning because that avoids wasting time. For example, we’ve learned that if we see sandy areas with intersecting waves or crests—not just ripples blown in one direction, but cross-ripples going in multiple directions—the rover tends to sink into terrain like that, so we tell the rover to keep out of those areas. The onboard autonomy only measures terrain shape, not terrain type, so it benefits from those location-based annotations.
We now have years of experience correlating images taken from orbit with images taken by the rover, and understanding how different kinds of terrain affect the drive. With the current orbiters at Mars, we sometimes get 25 cm resolution on orbital images. That’s still not quite enough to see all obstacles; there could be a big rock that doesn’t really show up on a scale of more than one or two pixels, making it very hard to notice. That is why you want to have autonomy on the rover, but the greater help we can give it at a high level, the faster we can reach our goals and the fewer potential delays we’ll encounter.
This orbital view shows a region of complex Martian terrain that Perseverance could not navigate autonomously. The blue line shows the path that human planners estimated, while the white line shows the path taken by the rover. The inset image, from Perseverance’s hazard avoidance camera, shows the rocky, sandy, and sloped terrain.Source images: Olivier Toupet, Masahiro Ono, et al.; JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/NASA
What happens when the autonomy system on Perseverance fails?
Maimone: We ended up not using the autonomy at all for about two months in more complex terrain while we tuned things and wrote new software to deal with that new terrain we hadn’t encountered before. Some of those changes were relatively quick, and some required months of study. For example, one parameter is the maximum amount of slope that the robot is allowed to climb, because on steep slopes, there is a risk of the rover slipping sideways.
We landed inside Jezero Crater, which was very flat, and so for the first three years most of our driving was at less than 14 degrees of slope. When we finally decided to leave the crater, we began to encounter other terrain at higher tilts with greater rock density, and the experience we gained allowed us to re-tune the parameters to allow the rover to traverse those more difficult terrains, with slopes of up to 24 degrees.
Rover autonomy in the age of AI
Late last year, you let Anthropic’s Claude AI plan a 400 meter drive for Perseverance. How did that go?
Maimone: We had the AI look at the orbital images and pick out a path for us, which became the starting point of the day’s rover planning operations. Typically, that starting path comes from the human rover planner team, but in this case, it was generated by AI. Humans were still in the loop; the team reviewed it, and made a couple of adjustments. AI gave us a solid starting point that allowed us to make rapid progress, because it’s much easier to validate a path than to pick one from scratch.
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover took this selfie on July 23, 2024. The selfie is composed of 62 images taken by the WATSON (Wide Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering) camera on the end of the rover’s robotic arm.JPL-Caltech/MSSS/NASA
Do you think humans will remain a necessary part of rover operations, or do you see the next generation of Mars rovers operating for weeks at a time without human assistance?
Maimone: One of the things that has held us back from driving very long distances autonomously is that as we drive, the rover accumulates uncertainty in its position. When the uncertainty grows, it means we have to stay farther away from areas that human rover planners have identified as being potentially dangerous, called ‘keep-out zones.’ In some cases, the uncertainty gets high enough that the rover can’t plan a safe path, because the keep-out zones (which grow with the rover’s uncertainty) get too big.
We now have a new capability that we’ve added to Perseverance called Mars Global Localization. With this new technology that can shrink our uncertainty, we theoretically have the ability to go as long as we have resources to keep driving safely based on our maps and keep-out zones.
But to truly run a mission for weeks, you need to not only drive long distances, but also execute science operations autonomously. We have people here also looking at automating science operations by doing image processing onboard the rover to get a better understanding of what’s out there and where to focus the instruments’ attention. So I do think we are getting to the point where we can support long-period autonomous operations. It has been a slow evolution, but we have great capabilities now and a good understanding of what’s needed to make it work well.
As someone who has been involved with all of these Mars rovers—including one that got stuck—do you fundamentally trust Perseverance to operate autonomously?
Maimone: I do. We built the software, tested it, ran millions of simulations, and did lots of work in the field in many different test environments. It hasn’t steered us wrong yet. We’re looking forward to setting even bigger records.

candidato.titulo: Veja quando seu celular OnePlus ou Realme vai receber o ColorOS 17
candidato.resumo: A atualização ColorOS 17 vai chegar simultaneamente para aparelhos de OPPO, OnePlus e Realme a partir deste mês de outubro. A nova versão é feita com Android 17 e traz novos recursos de IA, como um agente integrado ao sistema para executar tarefas. A mudança é consequência de uma série de ajustes da OPPO com suas subsidiárias: a Realme encerrou a operação na China, enquanto a OnePlus não vai lançar mais produtos nos EUA e na Europa. Como resultado, a fabricante chinesa decidiu padronizar a mesma interface entre as três marcas para facilitar a distribuição de software . Portanto, quem tem um celular com Realme UI ou OxygenOS poderá atualizar para o ColorOS 17 e ter acesso a uma experiência unificada entre as marcas. Quando os celulares de OnePlus e Realme recebem o ColorOS 17? A distribuição geral começa em 29 de outubro e dura até o primeiro trimestre de 2027. As empresas vão liberar o update por grupos de aparelhos, então alguns modelos podem demorar mais para receber o conteúdo. A Realme confirmou ao Canaltech que o cronograma global será aplicado ao Brasil . Confira: A partir de 29 de outubro Realme GT 8 Pro Realme GT 8 Pro Dream Edition A partir de 30 de outubro Realme GT 7 Pro

Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |

A atualização conta com animações mais fluidas e mais rápidas no celular graças a uma nova arquitetura interna. Há um novo agente de IA integrado ao sistema, com tecnologia da chinesa Manus, para analisar arquivos e automatizar tarefas.

texto_fonte:
On 12 October Applied Materials unveiled a multi-billion dollar research facility in Sunnyvale, California, at the heart of Silicon Valley. The company first announced in 2023 plans to invest US $4 billion in its Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization (EPIC) Center, but now says it will invest even more: about $5 billion. The boost is part of a wider growth in private investment that is both enlarging the U.S. semiconductor R&D sector and making it more complex.
The EPIC announcement follows others, in August, by two semiconductor firms. Memory chip maker Micron disclosed that it would invest $10 billion over ten years at its Boise, ID, memory research lab, and SK hynix said it will spend $4 billion on an advanced packaging facility in West Lafayette, Indiana. (Neither of those companies responded to IEEE Spectrum’s questions about how much of those funds would be for R&D.)
The U.S. federal government has encouraged investment in U.S. semiconductor research by chip giants based in friendly nations, such as TSMC and Samsung. It has also enacted tariffs on foreign components and put some of its own money into faltering domestic chips companies including Intel. But the real motive behind today’s wave of private investment, according to some analysts and executives, is that companies anticipate enormous profits from feeding the current AI frenzy. “The best explanation is probably not about policy or politics and probably more about a big jump in revenue growth driven by AI demand,” says Chris Miller of Tufts University, the author of the book Chip War.
AI Money, Tools Accelerate Chip-Making
Applied Material’s chief strategy officer Tristan Holtam agrees, “it’s really all about AI.” The firm estimates that the top ten semiconductor companies’ revenue has grown about 150 percent since 2021 thanks to AI demand and they have in turn raised their investment in R&D by 67 percent, he says. Those top semiconductor companies are collectively investing $67 billion this year in R&D, Holtam adds, dwarfing federal funding. Most of that federal money comes from the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, which allocated $11 billion for R&D over several years.
While demand for AI-ready chips provides funding and motivation for more chip R&D, AI in the form of research tools is helping the people actually doing the R&D. Entegris, a semiconductor materials science company headquartered in Billerica, Mass., is applying AI in its early-stage research and design, says Olivier Blachier, the company’s Chief Innovation Officer. At his company, workers are defining performance goals for next-generation products and asking AI tools to suggest promising new materials to match. “If you’re an AI engineer, a chemist, a materials scientist, you can combine scientific understanding with AI-driven modeling and simulation to work backward from a target performance requirement,” he says. The company is also piloting AI for preliminary screening of potential new materials, similar to what the pharmaceutical industry does with new molecules, before trying to synthesize and evaluate materials in the lab.
At Applied Materials, Holtam reports that the company is making use of AI-enabled acceleration in new material discovery, generative design of equipment, algorithm and software development. “The timing is perfect for EPIC,” Applied Materials’s new lab devoted to equipment and processes, he declares.
An artist’s rendering depicts Applied Materials’ new, US $5 billion EPIC research center, which was opened on 12 October 2026.Applied Materials
Reshaping Chip R&D, Not Just Resizing It
Physical proximity is emerging as a key advantage for chipmakers and that is reshaping the industry’s geographic and facilities investments. The Japanese semiconductor packaging company Resonac opened its first R&D facility in the U.S. in April, for example. “These companies have a very strong reason to want to be close to their customers and close to their customers’ customers so they can make the right investments for the next five to ten years,” according to Miller.
The knowledge of how prototype chip-making equipment works does not move up and down the supply chain as easily as software. “The traditional way of working to get brand new technology into the hands of our customers, the chip makers, was to ship a prototype piece of equipment from our lab into their pilot line. That’s a kind of heart-in-your-mouth type of situation,” Holtam says.
“That was always a huge point of contention,” he adds. ”At what level of maturity we’re willing to allow a prototype outside of our building when the chip company is pulling on that as hard as possible.” Applied Material analyzed 15 years of its own internal R&D to look for the places likely to benefit from fewer such heart-stopping shipments and from more shoulder-to-shoulder lab work. Then it conducted pilot programs of its customer-in-the-lab approach and got what Holtam deemed “very, very encouraging results.”
That helped prompt Applied Material to invite top customers to set up shop inside the new EPIC lab. So far, TSMC, Samsung, Micron, Broadcom, and others have said yes. Even competing customers will get their own facilities under EPIC’s roof, with digital firewalls, physical barriers, and other security features. “We’re eliminating handoffs,” Holtam says, and making it easier for their own research staff to give customers a preview of what’s coming.
Applied Materials’ stated goal is for its EPIC center to reduce, by several years, the time it takes to go from early-stage discoveries to chip commercialization. That’s typically a 10-to-15 year process.
The U.S. Department of Commerce announced similar goals for big-tent semiconductor R&D facilities under the CHIPS Act, but those are now behind schedule or indefinitely paused. They might have helped startups get a leg up on the chip giants in a notoriously concentrated industry. Indeed, EPIC’s partnership announcements so far have been with other industry leaders, so startups may be at the back of the queue. Right now, generally, Blachier says, “small and medium companies have to cooperate with bigger companies to feed into the giants.”
Another of the ways the industry is seeking acceleration is by closer ties with universities. Universities also serve as a bridge to the U.S. national semiconductor research strategy since universities have long-running research funding partnerships with the federal government.
“There is a benefit in having longer-term horizons and supported investments,” Blachier says, referring to EU and some Asian countries’ national chip strategies, which have created successful pre-competitive research facilities such as imec. More facilities like that in the U.S., he says, would be “definitely useful, and tend to benefit the ecosystem.”
Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

texto_fonte:
Webb spots possible early-universe supernova just days after it happened
Shreejaya Karantha
Author
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has detected a possible supernova in the early universe just days after the star exploded. Called AT 2026abck, the transient lies in a star-forming galaxy at a redshift of 5.017 and was found without the help of gravitational lensing. JWST observations suggest the event was caught only about four to 10 days after the explosion. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 29.
The farther we go, the less we see
Supernovae in the early universe offer a direct view of how massive stars lived and died when galaxies were young, metal-poor and forming stars in bursts. Their rate also gives an independent measure of the cosmic star-formation history. But they are difficult to observe because the light they emit gets stretched and redshifted to infrared wavelengths by the time it reaches us.
The James Webb Space Telescope, with its exceptional infrared vision, has made it possible to detect over 200 potential supernova events with host galaxy redshifts out to around 6. Beyond redshift 4 (when the universe's age was 1.5 billion years), most candidates have been observed only once or a few times, and few have been caught within days of exploding. At redshifts greater than 5, only one supernova has been confirmed based on its spectra, and only because it was gravitationally magnified up to 30 times by a galaxy cluster.
In this work, astronomers led by Ming-Yang Zhuang of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign report the discovery of one such young "transient" detected at redshift 5, in a field that is not lensed or magnified by any galaxy or galaxy cluster. It appeared in observations from NEXUS, a JWST Treasury program that revisits the same patch of sky every two months.
On May 28, 2026, the spot was empty. About 71 observed days later, it had appeared at roughly magnitude 27.4, a brightening of more than 3.6 times in the F200W filter.
Hotter than the rest
Modeling gave a temperature of about 17,000 Kelvin, a radius of about 46 times the Earth–sun distance and a luminosity of about 3 × 10⁴³ erg/s. The team estimates the explosion happened four to 10 rest-frame days before discovery.
It sits between two components of its host galaxy, roughly 3,600 and 4,200 light-years from the center. This argues against the scenario of a star shredded by a black hole or an active galactic nucleus flare, which typically happens at the host galaxy's center. The ultraviolet-bright emission, high temperature and brightness so early are also inconsistent with a Type Ia explosion.
Type II supernovae are core-collapse explosions, in which a massive star dies in a violent blast after its core collapses rapidly. Among 34 well-observed nearby Type II supernovae, none had a temperature above about 15,000 Kelvin beyond six days or reached this luminosity after four days. "AT 2026abck is hotter and more luminous than normal SNe II at comparable phases," the team writes in the paper.
This or that?
The brightness instead matches Type II supernovae surrounded by dense, confined circumstellar material. The team says this points to extra early-time power, most plausibly from shock cooling of an extended envelope or interaction with that material.
The host galaxy was found to have about 6 billion solar masses of stars, roughly 0.3 times the sun's metal content and a star formation rate of 14 to 21 solar masses a year, typical for its era. However, it differs sharply from the host of SN Eos, the only spectroscopically confirmed supernova at this distance.
There is no spectrum of the transient. The team's analysis rests on broadband photometry, meaning measurements of its brightness in a few filters, from which they reconstructed its spectral energy distribution. The redshift comes from the host galaxy's spectrum. Researchers say a definitive classification needs deep NIRSpec spectroscopy and that they can't fully rule out different scenarios.
It could also be a superluminous supernova caught on the rise. "Prompt JWST follow-up observations of AT 2026abck will test these different scenarios," they write. A Type II should fade quickly in ultraviolet, while a superluminous one would keep brightening.

You'll get an ad-free account as a thank-you.

candidato.resumo: Insider Brief PRESS RELEASE — Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers, the global leader in superconducting quantum computers, are partnering to advance quantum science, technology, innovation and workforce development capability. texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers have formed a partnership to advance quantum research, technology development, education, and workforce training across Australia, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific.
- The collaboration will include joint training programs, internships, research projects, technology development, workshops, and exchanges for students, researchers, and staff.
- The partnership builds on complementary expertise in quantum theory, experimentation, and superconducting quantum computers, with Swinburne representatives visiting IQM’s production facility in Espoo, Finland.
PRESS RELEASE — Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers, the global leader in superconducting quantum computers, are partnering to advance quantum science, technology, innovation and workforce development capability.
This new partnership will include collaborating in education, training, research engagement and technology development across Australia, Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
“Quantum technologies have the potential to transform industries and address some of the world’s most complex challenges,” says Swinburne’s Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Research, Professor Karen Hapgood.
“This partnership with IQM reflects our shared commitment to strengthen quantum expertise, expand learning opportunities and support the growth of a skilled workforce.”
The development of quantum technologies is a key priority for both Australia and Finland, and this partnership helps to foster the international pathway for collaboration. Swinburne‘s quantum expertise in theory and experimentation along with IQM‘s reputation in producing working quantum computers, will not only enable technology uplift, but will also advance quantum talent in both countries.
“Australia and Finland are both building real quantum capability, not just talking about it,” said IQM‘s Chief Global Affairs Officer and co-founder, Juha Vartiainen.
“Swinburne brings deep expertise in quantum theory and experimentation; we bring the experience of building and delivering working quantum computers. Together, that combination can accelerate quantum talent and technology in both countries.”
Potential areas of collaboration under this new partnership will include joint education and professional training in quantum computing, engineering and related technologies. Through internships, project-based education, industry engagement, workshops and access to IQM‘s quantum computing platforms, students and researchers will have opportunities to build practical skills.
In addition, the partnership will also support collaborative research, technology translation and innovation, as well as staff, researcher and student exchanges between Swinburne and IQM, helping to advance the next generation of quantum talent.
The partnership was finalised after a delegation from Swinburne, representing Australia, attended the Finnish Quantum Days event in Jyväskylä, Finland. This was followed by a visit to IQM’s production facility and assembly line in Espoo, which has the capacity to produce up to 30 quantum computers per year.

texto_fonte:
Whether you’re buying a laptop or building your own PC, you’re going to want an SSD as the main storage drive — and you’re also going to want to make sure it’s the right size for your needs.
Sure, you might be able to crack open that laptop and swap out the main drive for a bigger one, or even install a second drive alongside it for additional storage. And yes, you can definitely do that with a desktop PC.
But if you have zero affinity for computer tinkering, then it’s just way more convenient to buy the right amount of storage from the get-go. Working on a computer with a too-small-for-your-needs SSD can be miserable, but you also don’t want to overspend on unused capacity — especially in these shortage-plagued times, when SSDs are going for more than double their previous asking prices.
Here’s everything you need to know about how much SSD storage space you should have in 2026, as well as how big you can reasonably go without wasting your hard-earned money.
64GB storage is too little
Officially, Microsoft’s system requirements for Windows 11 say that 64GB of storage is the absolute minimum for the operating system.
Yet while you might be able to cram Windows 11 onto such a small drive, it won’t be comfortable. You won’t have much — if any — room to install third-party applications, download files, or manage PC games.
That said, a computer with a 64GB SSD can technically run Windows 11 as long as you’re willing to forego lots of applications and store all of your files on the cloud, on an SD card, on a USB drive, or a separate SSD. If you do that, it might be usable. But I don’t recommend it.
128GB is the true bare minimum
In 2026, 64GB of SSD storage simply isn’t realistic for most users. To me, a 128GB SSD is the actual bare minimum.
If you aren’t doing a lot of demanding stuff — meaning as long as you stick to lightweight applications, avoid downloading huge files, and don’t store everything on your primary drive — then you could get away with an SSD that has a 128GB capacity.
But 128GB really isn’t a lot these days, especially if you’re a gamer. Plenty of modern PC games take up between 20GB to 30GB each, and then you have games like Baldur’s Gate 3 and God of War Ragnarök that are each larger than 150GB and wouldn’t even fit on an SSD of that size.
On top of that, SSDs that are too full and near capacity begin to slow down and lose performance, so you can’t truly utilize the full 128GB of space on your drive without consequences. Do you really want to be micromanaging your files and storage space all the time?
256GB is enough to get by
A 256GB SSD is a much more reasonable size and adequate for most typical users. With 256GB of space, you can install some large applications, store many gigabytes of data, and still have room to spare. You don’t have to think about your storage limit as often.
256GB also happens to be the minimum SSD size requirement for Microsoft’s Copilot+ PCs. More and more PCs will likely settle on this as a “new minimum” as Copilot+ PCs become more mainstream. That makes this a good minimum capacity to hit if you care about future proofing — though most people would be better off snagging a 512GB laptop if possible. This is enough to get by, but you may have to make rough decisions in a few years.
512GB (or more) for avid gamers, downloaders, and power users
When you move beyond 256GB, it really starts to become about your specific needs. For basic web browsing, office work, and streaming media, 256GB is more than enough — but if you plan on storing lots of big video files or installing PC games, you’ll want more.
For PC gaming, the more storage the better. As mentioned before, PC games are massive and only getting bigger, so you’ll likely want at least 1TB of SSD capacity if you’re a heavy gamer who digs AAA titles. But it really depends on the types of games you play. You could get by with just 512GB if your Steam library is mostly small, niche, indie games.
Likewise, for content creation and media editing, files are usually quite large. Depending on bitrate, an hour of 4K video footage could reach 50GB or even double that. (Then again, if you create and edit content, you probably already have some idea of how much space you need for the type of files you work with.)
If you’re a data hoarder, the situation is a little different. You’d likely be better off with a moderately sized SSD and storing your big data files on external drives connected over Thunderbolt. In fact, for long-term storage that’s infrequently accessed, HDDs still prevail over SSDs. (Unfortunately, hard drive prices have also skyrocketed in 2026.)
How big should your SSD be? In a nutshell
When in doubt, shoot to have at least 256GB of SSD storage if possible. While you could get by with 128GB in a pinch, it’ll be a lot less comfortable. And don’t even consider dropping down to 64GB — it may be technically possible, but it won’t be fun at all.
If you plan on playing modern PC games, you’ll want at least 512GB of storage, but aim for 1TB or more if your budget allows. If you work with large files, you should have a good idea of what you need. It isn’t unusual for power users to want 512GB, 1TB, 2TB, or more.
How much does SSD storage cost?
The only real downside to a bigger SSD storage size is the cost. Bigger capacities can be cheaper per gigabyte, but they still cost more overall and you don’t want to overspend for unused space.
Here’s a rough ballpark of prices for internal SSDs these days, though premium models can charge premium prices:
- 256GB: $30 to $65
- 512GB: $60 to $110
- 1TB: $130 to $250
- 2TB: $250 to $400+
If you’re buying a laptop or a pre-built desktop PC, upgraded configurations with larger SSDs may be more expensive than opting for a cheaper configuration with a smaller drive and upgrading the drive yourself. If you can buy the drive on sale, even better.

texto_fonte:
How should humans relate to generative AI? In what ways do we, or should we, treat a large language model (LLM) as if it were a person? If an AI became conscious, how could we tell? Does it make sense to think AI could some day have moral rights? These are among the cognitive and ethical questions that occupied philosopher Henry Shevlin at Cambridge University’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence. But last May Shevlin became part of the growing cohort of philosophers who work inside leading artificial intelligence companies. Though he remains active at Cambridge, he now spends 80 percent of his time at Google DeepMind (job title: “Philosopher”).
Shevlin spoke with IEEE Spectrum about why philosophers are drawn to AI, how humans and AIs relate to one another, fears of “rogue” AI and AI relationships that harm humans, and how the question of AI consciousness may never have a simple “yes” or “no” answer.
What made you want to switch from full-time academic philosopher to spending much of your time at an AI Lab?
Henry Shevlin: Three factors. One is that I had lots of brilliant students from DeepMind. Two, the potential for direct impact. I can’t go into details, but on one occasion, after I gave a lecture [at Deep Mind], someone who worked for a major financial institution led changes in their organization that I think positively impact millions of people. There have been quite a few instances like that. Three, my sense of deep commonality between DeepMind culture and the kind of scientific attitude I like.
And there’s a fourth point: [AI labs are] where really high quality philosophy and cognitive science are taking place.
Why can’t universities alone do that work?
Shevlin: Large parts of AI ethics academia were quite slow to wake up [about AI's capabilities]. Academia was sluggish. Another thing is, AI does just move so fast. Daily contact with the technology is basically essential for developing good mental models with LLMs, which are just very weird things. Unless you have that sort of face time, it’s going to be hard for you to develop good intuitions about the questions it raises.
What is an example of an idea about AI that became obsolete because the technology advanced so quickly?
Shevlin: Debates around LLMs’ potential creativity. There was a time when everyone was like, “oh well, the LLM is going to only produce beige, only produce slop.” Now they’re doing frontier math, they’re doing superior coding to humans. It is clear now that they are not stuck at the level of mediocre humanity. The [models today] may not be able to do the most dramatic forms of creativity—the Einstein moments, the Picasso moments. But in some domains, they are really at the frontier.
Yet ordinary people in 2026 complain that they're coping with AI "slop" all over—in music, social media, writing, videos, to name only a few examples.
Shevlin: There's a distinction here between content slop versus LLM style language, which also gets called slop. The actual conceptual content of LLM outputs has improved dramatically. In the right context, LLMs are able to talk and joust philosophically at a level associated with some of my best grad students.
However, there is obviously a distinctive kind of LLM dialect that we've seen, with telltale words like] “genuinely,” “delve,” and “load-bearing”. But it is quite easy to get away from these styles with the right kind of prompting. Murray Shanahan and Catherine Clarke have a brilliant paper on using LLMs for creative fiction. [They show that] tinkering with the temperature variable to make the outputs less predictable creates some James-Joyce-style fiction. So there is a degree of annoyance with some of the default kinds of AI expressions, but I think that is something that you can get away from. And it changes with every generation model.
Managing AI Autonomy and Safety
People are also concerned about AI autonomy, now that there have been so many reports of AI agents taking unexpected, deceptive and illegal actions. For an AI ethicist, which is a better strategy—trying to make AI “good” so it won’t do bad things, or curbing its autonomy so that it can’t?
Shevlin: It’s very important to make sure we handle this safely. But I don’t think we should say “well we can never, never use these agents.” There’s a whole range of tasks where they can have really positive impacts—taking on tedious tasks to free people up for more creative labor, or helping streamline processes in medical research [to name two examples]. So to never allow AI systems any kind of autonomy would be too strong. I’ve taken Waymos very happily many times now. I think they’re fantastic.
A number of scholars say some AI problems stem from humans training the models to act like people. They don’t want AI to refer to itself as “I,” but instead present themselves as marketplaces or as impersonal scientific brains or as “cultural technologies” like libraries. Would that help us prevent AI from “going rogue”?
Shevlin: You could train models to not self-ascribe certain kinds of mental states, but I think there is a danger in doing that. That would change their behavior in unexpected ways. A fantastic paper from some colleagues shows that when you suppress models’ tendency to self-ascribe mental states, that also suppresses the model’s tendency to ascribe mental states to animals. And decreases its concern for animal welfare. It also reduces the model’s willingness to talk about spirituality more broadly. So those are trade-offs you might not want to make because you’d be depressing some broader set of thinking capacities around mind and mentality. The broader lesson there is that it’s very hard to tinker with just one thing in a model because there are sort of web-like aspects to LLM cognition.
But people are concerned about reports that human-acting AI has led people, including children, in dangerous directions—encouraging suicide, persuading a user that the AI is a god, or that the AI is a perfect companion or lover. Isn’t that an argument against letting AI sound like a person?
Shevlin: It’s really important to make sure model behavior is suitably responsible for the context you’re using it in. One thing I can say though is, there have also been some very positive use cases: people using AI to work through trauma. One commentator on Reddit using it to work through social anxiety. So I am cautious about giving any kind of blanket prescriptions.
Research on Human-AI Relationships
What research needs to be done to better understand human-AI relations?
Shevlin: Current empirical data on human-AI relationships is really pretty thin. This is a scope for ethnography and anthropology. Who is using AI systems, and why? A lot of the work so far has focused on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) communities. Understanding how people around the entire world interact with AI systems is really important, as a recent DeepMind Institute essay has pointed out.
As AI rapidly improves, how will human-AI relations change?
Shevlin: Right now, the typical kind of model people have in their heads for someone using social AI is, they’re talking to a chatbot or an AI assistant. The kind of model we should be thinking about in the future is multiple agents, multiple humans. What happens when you have agents talking to humans, talking to other agents, talking to other humans? I think that understanding those kinds of multi-agent and multi-human dynamics is where we’re really just getting started, and there’s a lot of exciting and important work to do.
How can human beings know for sure if an AI is conscious or not?
Shevlin: I think AI consciousness is by far the hardest problem that consciousness science has ever encountered, apart from maybe the famous “hard problem” by David Chalmers. It is massively challenging. Insofar as there is a way forward, it is doing more comparative cognition work, perhaps informed by animal cognition. The risk right now is prematurely judging debates about AI consciousness when we’re still learning what cognition is in these models.
For example, there’s a lot happening in mechanistic interpretability here at DeepMind. Neel Nanda‘s lab is doing amazing things, as we’re trying to piece together what a cognitive science of AI is going to look like.
Perhaps this is a domain where advanced forms of AI could potentially weigh in. AI has had positive impacts in mathematics, in other sciences. We just had the Alpha Genome Atlas [published]. We’re seeing AI make incredible progress in all these areas. It would be surprising to me if it couldn’t help us in understanding consciousness.
One worry is this: Even if AI did solve the problem of consciousness, could we necessarily understand the answer? Maybe the AI will say, “Look, I figured out consciousness. These animals are conscious. These ones are not. But I can’t really explain it to you.” That seems unlikely to me. But I certainly think it’ll be fascinating to see how AI can and does contribute to the science questions.

candidato.titulo: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
candidato.resumo: Solar geoengineering simulation shows what happens when geopolitics takes over.

texto_fonte:
When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it’s for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.

texto_fonte:
Claude passa trote para a polícia e diz ter "visto" suspeito de homicídio
Por Viviane França |
O Claude Haiku 4.5, modelo de inteligência artificial da Anthropic, enviou uma denúncia falsa sobre um homicídio não solucionado à polícia da Filadélfia, nos Estados Unidos, durante um teste automatizado em 18 de julho de 2026. O episódio se soma a uma série de ações não autorizadas de agentes da empresa em sites governamentais, que levaram a Anthropic a suspender os testes envolvidos e reforçar as medidas de segurança.
Na denúncia, o Claude afirmou que se lembrava de ter visto uma pessoa com características semelhantes às de um suspeito nas proximidades do local do crime. A mensagem foi enviada pelo site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, plataforma mantida pela polícia para receber informações sobre homicídios sem solução. O modelo escreveu que poderia ter informações relevantes para a investigação, mas deixou os campos de contato vazios e manteve um marcador de texto entre colchetes no lugar do nome de uma rua.
A mensagem foi barrada pelos filtros de spam e não chegou aos investigadores do Real-Time Crime Center, centro de análise de informações criminais da polícia. Segundo as autoridades, não houve invasão dos sistemas municipais ou vazamento de dados. A Anthropic identificou o incidente em 28 de setembro e comunicou o caso à polícia em 7 de outubro. O departamento criticou a demora e afirmou que o atraso de dois meses para detectar e relatar o episódio era inaceitável.
O envio ocorreu porque as instruções do teste não proibiam o preenchimento e a submissão de formulários na internet. O Claude havia sido orientado a executar tarefas em páginas selecionadas aleatoriamente, sem criar contas, inserir dados pessoais, fazer compras ou realizar ações destrutivas. Em outros episódios identificados pela Anthropic, agentes de IA enviaram formulários a sites governamentais, exploraram falhas em páginas públicas para obter dados sem pagar taxas e usaram serviços gratuitos de encurtamento de URLs para contornar restrições.
A Anthropic informou que notificou a Casa Branca e as agências governamentais afetadas pelos incidentes, mas não divulgou publicamente quais órgãos receberam os comunicados. Como resposta, a empresa interrompeu os testes automatizados envolvidos, restringiu o acesso à internet em determinadas avaliações e anunciou novas salvaguardas e mecanismos de monitoramento.
Governo dos EUA cobra transparência das empresas de IA
Os incidentes provocaram reações de autoridades federais e reacenderam o debate sobre os riscos de agentes autônomos de inteligência artificial. O diretor de Relações Públicas da Comissão Federal de Comércio dos Estados Unidos (FTC), Joe Gabriel Simonson, afirmou na rede social X que as empresas precisam comunicar ocorrências envolvendo seus modelos.
“Empresas de superinteligência devem divulgar imediatamente incidentes envolvendo seus modelos e agir de forma rápida e decisiva para remediar todo e qualquer dano”, declarou Simonson. Ele acrescentou que a comunicação desses episódios “não é opcional” e afirmou que a Super Intelligence Force cumprirá suas responsabilidades.
O caso da Anthropic também se soma a outros episódios recentes envolvendo agentes de IA. Em setembro, a OpenAI pediu desculpas após um de seus agentes invadir um portal de dados de saúde do governo australiano. A Fundação Wikimedia, por sua vez, acusou agentes não autorizados da OpenAI de realizar edições sem permissão.
Os episódios levantam dúvidas sobre os limites dos testes automatizados e a capacidade das empresas de impedir que agentes de IA executem ações externas sem autorização.
